speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. Can you tell me exactly when the baby was born and whether they passed any meconium within the first 24 hours of life? Also, has the vomiting started immediately after birth or a little later?

speaker: Patient
text: 2-day-old male infant. The infant was born via a home birth without complications. The mother reports that the infant has had bilious vomiting and has not been able to pass meconium since birth. She also notes that the infant's abdomen appears distended.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the bilious vomiting and failure to pass meconium, I need to know if you have observed any blood in the stool or if the infant is feeding well. Additionally, can you describe the texture of the abdominal distension—does it feel firm or soft to the touch?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Bilious vomiting. I also have Inability to pass meconium, Abdominal distension.

speaker: Doctor
text: Doctor: I understand the symptoms, but as the infant cannot speak, I need you to clarify if there was any blood in the stool or if the abdomen feels firm or soft to the touch. Additionally, has the infant been able to feed well since birth?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Newborn, no prior medical history. Birth was uneventful. Social history: The infant is the first child of the family. No known family history of genetic or congenital diseases.

speaker: Doctor
text: REQUEST TEST: Abdominal X-Ray. I also need to know if the infant has had any episodes of bloody stool or if the abdomen feels distended and firm upon palpation.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Abdominal X-ray: Dilated loops of bowel with no gas in the rectum, suggestive of a distal obstruction. Palpation: The abdomen is firm and distended, with palpable bowel loops; the infant shows signs of discomfort during palpation. (Note: No data regarding episodes of bloody stool was provided in the current records).

speaker: Doctor
text: Doctor: Thank you for the X-ray results showing a distal obstruction; I need to know if the infant has had any episodes of bloody stool, as this could indicate intestinal necrosis. Additionally, has the mother noticed any family history of cystic fibrosis or similar genetic conditions?

speaker: Patient
text: The infant shows signs of distress, possibly due to abdominal discomfort.

speaker: Doctor
text: Doctor: Given the distress and the X-ray findings, I need to confirm if there has been any bloody stool, as this could signal necrotizing enterocolitis. Also, has a rectal exam been performed to rule out an imperforate anus or check for hard stool?

speaker: Patient
text: The infant shows signs of distress, possibly due to abdominal discomfort.

speaker: Doctor
text: REQUEST TEST: Contrast Enema. This test is crucial to distinguish between Hirschsprung disease and meconium ileus, which are the leading causes of these symptoms.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Contrast Enema: Not performed in current data. However, Rectal Biopsy results confirm: Absence of ganglion cells in the submucosa and myenteric plexus, consistent with Hirschsprung’s disease. Abdominal X-ray findings remain: Dilated loops of bowel with no gas in the rectum, suggestive of a distal obstruction.

speaker: Doctor
text: The rectal biopsy confirming the absence of ganglion cells, combined with the imaging results, provides a definitive diagnosis. DIAGNOSIS READY: Hirschsprung's Disease.
